summary:
TerraLens starts from a place and finds what is really changing there. Pick one of five regions (Ireland, Iberia, the Sahel, NW South Asia or the US Southwest), and TerraLens tests five NASA Earth-science variables over 1980–2025: air temperature, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, precipitation and aerosol, all from MERRA-2 via NASA GES DISC. It ranks what is changing, shows how fast with a 95% confidence interval, and gives each variable a plain verdict. We adjust every p-value with the Benjamini–Hochberg method to keep false discoveries.

Opposite Trends puts two places side by side: US Southwest rainfall is falling while NW South Asia’s is rising. The Time Machine shows how the verdict changes with the years you choose, and how long a record would be needed to detect a trend that isn’t proven yet.

This covers every step the challenge asks for: choosing variables, getting regional data, building long time series, and measuring both the rate and the significance of each trend. It matters because charting tools draw a trend line without saying whether it is real. TerraLens tells students and the public what is changing, how sure we can be, and when the honest answer is “not proven yet”.
details:
What it does and how it works. TerraLens starts from a place, not a variable. Choose one of five study regions in contrasting pairs: Ireland, Iberia, the Sahel, NW South Asia or the US Southwest. TerraLens shows five NASA Earth-science variables there over 1980 to 2025: air temperature, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, precipitation and aerosol optical depth. All five come from NASA’s MERRA-2 reanalysis. Each variable is averaged over the region’s box, one value per month. Each calendar month’s normal is removed so the seasons don’t look like a trend, and the result is tested with a seasonal Mann–Kendall test, corrected because neighbouring months are not independent. Sen’s slope gives the rate per decade with a 95% confidence interval. Because five variables are tested at once, every p-value is adjusted (Benjamini–Hochberg), and each variable gets one plain verdict: Significant, Weak evidence, No clear trend or Not enough data. Three views use these results. The Lineup ranks what is changing in a place. Opposite Trends compares one variable across two places: US Southwest rainfall falls 23 mm per decade while NW South Asia’s rises 66 mm. The Time Machine lets users change the years and watch the verdict respond, and for unproven trends it shows how long a record detection would need.

Benefits. It is honest by design: it says “not proven yet” instead of drawing a convincing line. It is readable by students and the public, with plain definitions and a verdict before any p-value, and the full evidence is one click away. Every number traces back to a NASA source file, and the same statistics ship as a Python package, terralens-earth, so anyone can reproduce them.

Intended impact. We want people to learn that evidence has a strength: a trend can be real, uncertain or not yet detectable, and the years you choose matter. We hope TerraLens leads students on to NASA tools such as Giovanni.

Tools and technologies. Data comes from NASA MERRA-2 v5.12.4 via GES DISC, Giovanni and Harmony. GPM IMERG, GLDAS-2.1, NASA POWER and NOAA ground stations serve as cross-checks. The analysis runs in Python with pandas, NumPy, xarray, SciPy, statsmodels and harmony-py, with pymannkendall used to validate our statistics, plus FastAPI, Pydantic, pytest and Ruff. The web app uses JavaScript with React, Vite, Recharts, MapLibre GL and React Router. It is hosted on Cloudflare Pages, with GitHub Actions for automated checks and Linear for planning. We used Claude Code, Codex and Codebuff for code and drafts, and ElevenLabs for the demo narration; all of this is declared in the repository. Hardware: team laptops only.

Creativity. TerraLens reverses the usual order: instead of charting the trend you already suspected, it scans many variables and finds the suspects. It turns three statistical ideas into views students can use: correcting for testing many things at once, how the time window changes the answer, and how long a record must be to detect a trend.

Factors we considered. Scientific honesty came first: no forecasts, no causal claims, and “no clear trend” never shown as “no change”. We chose a long, consistent record that is long enough to detect trends, and kept shorter satellite and land-model data as independent checks. We validated our results against ground stations and satellite data, and our statistics against an independent library. We served precomputed results so nothing can fail live.
dataRefs: MERRA-2 M2TMNXSLV v5.12.4: monthly 2 m air temperature (T2M)
MERRA-2 M2TMNXLND v5.12.4: monthly land surface diagnostics (soil moisture SFMC, evapotranspiration EVLAND)
MERRA-2 M2TMNXFLX v5.12.4: monthly surface fluxes (bias-corrected precipitation PRECTOTCORR)
MERRA-2 M2TMNXAER v5.12.4: monthly aerosol diagnostics (aerosol optical depth TOTEXTTAU)
GPM IMERG Final Precipitation L3 Monthly V07 (GPM_3IMERGM)
GLDAS-2.1 Noah Land Surface Model L4 Monthly 0.25° (GLDAS_NOAH025_M)
NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
NASA Giovanni (GES DISC online visualisation and analysis)
NASA Harmony (Earthdata subsetting and transformation service)
